newsitem.title: USA: Republicans chip away at Democrats in South.
newsitem.headline: Republicans chip away at Democrats in South.

text.p: Republicans chipped away at traditional Democratic strongholds in the South Tuesday, capturing two new U.S. Senate seats while adding a handful of House districts in their bid to retain control of Congress.

Even before President Bill Clinton claimed his own re-election victory, Arkansas Republican Representative Tim Hutchison had scored a coup by winning election as the first Republican senator from the state in more than 100 years.

Alabama state attorney general Jeff Sessions also brought the Republican party another victory, overcoming Democratic state Sen. Roger Bedford in the race to fill the seat being vacated by retiring veteran Democrat Howell Heflin.
"Today, the working people of this state have spoken. They want a conservative, responsible, family-values senator," Sessions told supporters while claiming victory in the Gulf city of Mobile.
Alabama and Arkansas were two of four states where retiring Democratic incumbents had left their party vulnerable to Republican takeover.
The victories helped shatter Democratic hopes of reclaiming the Senate by giving Republicans a net two-seat gain in the nationwide race.

Before the election, Republicans held a 53-47 majority in the U.S. Senate. Democrats needed to gain three seats to take control of the Senate because Vice President Al Gore would cast the deciding vote in the Senate in the event of a tie.
But in the other two Southern states with open Senate seats -- Louisiana and Georgia -- Democrats managed to hold their ground.
In Louisiana, Democrat Mary Landrieu captured the Senate race from conservative Republican Louis "Woody" Jenkins after campaigning as an abortion rights supporter in the heavily Catholic state.
Democrat Max Cleland also was the winner in Georgia, where he narrowly overcame an aggressive challenge from Republican businessman Guy Millner.
Meanwhile, Southern Republicans successes were less auspicious in their battle to help spoil Democratic attempts to take control of the House of Representatives.
But House Speaker Newt Gingrich confidently predicted that the region would play a key role in maintaining the Republican majority.
"It looks, as of right now, like we will almost certainly keep control of the United States House of Representatives," the Georgia Republican told supporters in his own district.
To offset expected losses in other parts of the country, Republicans targeted 17 open Southern House seats, where Democratic incumbents were retiring.
But experts expected them to pick up less than half a dozen of the open seats.

With results still coming in, Republicans scored expected victories in the 3rd congressional districts of Alabama and Mississippi, where candidates took advantage of a strong shift towards the party of Lincoln.
They also captured the fifth districts of Louisiana and Texas. But Democrats clawed back the turf they lost in two districts in North Carolina.
